summary: Extends the SIP REFER method, which asks a recipient to contact a URI, by adding a Referred-By header that tells the recipient who made the referral. This is useful for call transfer and for authenticating who asked for it.

eli5.summary: When someone says "call this person," the Referred-By header tells the person who sent you, so they know who to blame.

questions: what is the sip referred-by header
how does sip call transfer identify the referrer
subtitle: How a SIP call transfer tells the final recipient who asked for it, and how to stop the middleman faking it.

tldr.problem: When a SIP user agent is asked to contact someone (a REFER), nothing tells the target that the request was a referral or who made it, so the target cannot tell it from any other request.
tldr.mechanism: The referrer adds a Referred-By header carrying its SIP URI, and optionally a signed (and possibly encrypted) S/MIME token. The referee copies both unchanged into the request it sends to the refer target. A new 429 response lets a target demand a valid token.
tldr.outcome: Targets can base admission decisions on who made the referral, and can detect a referee that forges or reuses the information. The protection is optional, and the referee can still delete all of it. The RFC is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 8217.

facts.label: Header parameter
facts.value: cid, the Content-ID of the token

today: RFC 3892 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 8217. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Referrals Need an Identity
sections.content:
The SIP REFER method (RFC 3515) lets one party, the referrer, hand a second party, the referee, a URI to contact. If it is a SIP URI, the referee sends a request, often an INVITE, to it. That destination is the refer target. Nothing in RFC 3515 makes the referenced request look different from any other request the referee might have sent.

Some uses, such as call transfer, benefit from telling the target who made the referral, what URI was referred to, and when. The target can use this when deciding whether to accept the request. This RFC defines one set of mechanisms for that.

All of them work by putting information in the REFER that the referee copies into the referenced request. That makes the referee an eavesdropper on the information, and puts it in a position to attack it. At its simplest the RFC defines a new Referred-By header carrying the referrer's identity as a SIP URI. On top of that it defines an S/MIME based token that lets the target detect tampering.
sections.eli5: When you are sent to someone by a friend, that person cannot normally tell. This RFC gives your friend a way to attach a note saying who sent you.

sections.title: Who Does What
sections.content:
The referrer provides a Referred-By header holding its SIP address-of-record, and may attach an S/MIME protected token that reflects its identity and the details of the REFER. The referee copies the header and the token, if any, into the triggered request.

Referrer. It MAY include a Referred-By header, but a REFER MUST NOT carry more than one. If it includes a token, the header MUST have a cid parameter equal to the Content-ID of the body part holding the token. After a 429 it MAY send a new REFER with a token.

Referee. It MUST copy any Referred-By value and token into the referenced request without modification. It MAY reject a REFER that lacks a token with a 429, but SHOULD NOT reject a token merely because it is encrypted to a key it does not hold. It SHOULD present the same identity to the referrer and the target.

Refer target. A request with no Referred-By is handled by the ordinary SIP rules. If the header is present, the target MAY apply extra admission policy. Because the referee can alter the header, or invent one when no REFER exists, the target SHOULD require a valid token if forgery could affect its policy. Without a token it MAY proceed, but any information it shows its user MUST be flagged as suspect. It MUST reject a request with an invalid token with a 429.
sections.eli5: There are three people: the friend who sends you, you in the middle, and the person at the door. You have to pass the note along exactly as written, and the person at the door gets to decide how much to trust it.

sections.title: The Referred-By Header Field
sections.content:
Referred-By is a request header that can appear in any request, though it is meaningless for ACK and CANCEL. It has a compact form, b. It carries the referrer's SIP URI and optionally a cid parameter naming the Content-ID of the body part that holds the token.

The cid value is written in double quotes in the header. To get the Content-ID used in the MIME body, replace the quotes with angle brackets. So cid="2UWQFN309shb3@ref.example" points at the body part with Content-ID: <2UWQFN309shb3@ref.example>.

If the URI contains a comma, question mark or semicolon, it MUST be enclosed in angle brackets. Proxies do not need to read the header and MUST NOT remove or modify it.
sections.eli5: It is a label on the request that says 'sent by this person', plus an optional pointer to the sealed proof that goes with it.

sections.title: The Referred-By Token
sections.content:
The token is an Authenticated Identity Body as defined in RFC 3893, identified by a MIME Content-ID. It is a signed message/sipfrag that MUST contain copies of the Refer-To, Referred-By and Date header fields from the REFER. It SHOULD NOT contain Call-ID (not useful to the target and possibly an information leak) or From (the claimed identity is already in Referred-By). It MAY be encrypted as well as signed.

The To header MAY be included, but SHOULD NOT be unless the referrer has cryptographically identified the referee, for example by checking the certificate of a TLS connection or by encrypting the Refer-To. If the certificate matches only the hostname, the referrer's user should be asked for consent first.

The target MUST treat a token with an invalid signature as invalid, and SHOULD treat one with an aged Date as invalid. It SHOULD check that the request matches the Refer-To in the token, at least the method and any end-to-end headers, and that the identity in the token matches the signing certificate's subjectAltName.
sections.eli5: The token is the sealed envelope with a signature. It says who asked, for what, and when, so the person at the door can check the note was not changed or reused.

sections.title: The 429 Provide Referrer Identity Response
sections.content:
A refer target uses the new 429 client error, suggested text "Provide Referrer Identity", to say the referee must provide a valid Referred-By token. The referee passes this back to the referrer in a NOTIFY carrying a message/sipfrag body. A referee that itself requires a token can answer the REFER directly with a 429.

The 428 response from the authenticated identity work is not appropriate here, because it is used to ask the referee for an authentication token. After a 429 the referrer may try again with a token.
sections.eli5: It is the door person saying 'I need to see the signed note first.' Then your friend can send a proper one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The referee is by design an eavesdropper and an ideal man-in-the-middle. The RFC notes that an endpoint's behavior can be entirely under one user's control, so a malicious referee is more feasible than a malicious proxy run by a service provider. The S/MIME protection is optional, and anyone skipping it needs their own defense against three risks:

  • The information probably influences admission policy (for example a prompt such as "This call was transferred to you by X. Accept?"), so a referee could falsify it. The signature hampers that.
  • The referee sees everything in it. Encryption addresses this.
  • The referee could store the information and paste it into later unrelated requests. Covering a timestamp and the Refer-To by the signature lets the target detect that.

Nothing prevents the referee from deleting all referred-by information, and the target cannot detect it. That turns the request into an ordinary SIP request, so the referee gains no new influence. Targets can defend against token removal by answering with 429.

A minimal token says who asked for what at what time, but not who was asked. That allows a cut-and-paste attack: if Mallory sees Alice refer Carol, he can copy the token into his own request. Including the To header closes this, at a privacy cost: Carol's identity is revealed, which defeats a wish for anonymity. Carol can protect herself by rejecting any REFER with a token she cannot inspect.
sections.eli5: The person in the middle could lie about the note, read it, or reuse an old one. The signature and the seal help the person at the door notice, but the middle person can still throw the note away.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives four message flows. The basic one shows a signed token travelling from the REFER into the INVITE. The insecure one omits the token: the header alone is copied through, and the target accepts it. In the third, the target requires a token, replies with a 429 that reaches the referrer as a NOTIFY, and the referrer retries with an encrypted token that succeeds.

The nested case has A refer B to send a REFER to C, which refers C to send an INVITE to D. A's token is passed through B and C to D, B does not add a token of its own, and A is notified about the outcome of the REFER at B, not of the INVITE at C.
sections.eli5: The examples show the note being passed along, being refused once because it had no signature, and then being accepted when it came with one.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The RFC registers a new SIP header field name with the compact form b, and a new client error response code, 429 "Provide Referrer Identity", under the Request Failure 4xx heading in the SIP parameters registry.
sections.eli5: The new header and the new error number were added to the official list so nobody else reuses them.

messages.label: REFER
messages.note: Refer-To plus Referred-By and, optionally, a token with a matching Content-ID.

messages.label: INVITE
messages.note: Copies Referred-By and the token without modification.

messages.label: 429 Provide Referrer Identity
messages.note: Only if the target requires a valid token.
